 Biodegradable cosmetic ingredients open new opportunities for India’s specialty chemical industry 
 Eastman has launched Esmeri SK1N10, a biodegradable cellulose ester micropowder that aims to make skincare feel better while helping sunscreens perform more effectively. It promises a softer finish, less shine and quicker dry-down.Why this matters: If you have ever hated sticky creams or greasy sunscreen, this is aimed at you. Eastman says the ingredient can work in serums, moisturisers and sunscreens, while supporting biodegradable, non-nano formulas that fit growing sustainability demands.
 Impact on India: Eastman’s biodegradable micropowder highlights growing demand for sustainable ingredients in skincare and sunscreens. For India’s specialty chemical manufacturers, this could create opportunities to develop biodegradable alternatives for personal care formulations. However, competing with established global suppliers will require investment in research, and product performance. ETChemicals

 Eastman is trying to solve one of personal care ’s hardest trade-offs: how to make skincare and sunscreen feel better on skin without leaning on ingredients that run counter to sustainability goals. The US materials company has introduced a new biodegradable micropowder that it says can improve texture, reduce shine and support sun protection performance in a single formulation. According to Indian Chemical News , the launch expands Eastman ’s Esmeri personal care line with Esmeri SK1N10 , a readily biodegradable, non-nano cellulose ester micropowder aimed at creams, serums, sprays and sun care products. The ingredient is designed for formulators who are under pressure to deliver sensory appeal, regulatory compliance and environmental credibility at the same time. A multifunctional ingredient for a crowded formulation brief Eastman says the new powder is intended for both aqueous and oil-in-water systems, giving brands a flexible ingredient for a wide range of personal care formats. The company claims the material delivers an immediate soft-focus effect, faster dry-down, lower tackiness and a soft matte finish that can make products feel lighter on application. That matters because consumer complaints often centre on exactly those points. In Eastman’s research involving 6,000 women and girls aged 12 to 70 across six countries, 45 per cent said they struggled to find facial skincare products that met all their needs. Sticky textures, greasy residue and weak visible results were among the main frustrations reported in the study. For formulators, those complaints translate into a commercial problem. Products that feel heavy or leave residue can struggle to win repeat purchases, even when they contain active ingredients with strong performance claims. Eastman is positioning SK1N10 as a way to help brands close that gap while also aligning with sustainability expectations. Why sunscreen makers are paying attention The ingredient’s most notable claim is its potential role in sun care. Eastman says the micropowder can enhance UV scattering, which may improve the performance of both organic and inorganic UV filters. In practical terms, that could create an SPF-boosting effect and potentially allow formulators to lower the concentration of UV filters while improving skin feel. That is a commercially relevant proposition because sunscreen makers are often caught between efficacy, aesthetics and consumer preference. Higher filter loads can improve protection, but they may also leave products feeling heavy, chalky or greasy. A powder that helps with dispersion and sensory performance could therefore be useful in both premium skincare and mass-market sun care. Eastman says the ingredient can be used in serums, creams, moisturisers, sprays, eye treatments and sunscreens, including formulations that contain active ingredients such as retinoids. That broad compatibility suggests the company is not targeting a niche effect, but a platform ingredient that can be built into multiple product types. Biodegradability is becoming a buying criterion The launch also reflects a wider shift in the personal care market, where biodegradability is moving from a specialist requirement to a mainstream expectation. In a survey of 150 research and development professionals at personal care consumer packaged goods and fast-moving consumer goods companies across 11 countries, nearly half expected biodegradable ingredients to become mainstream in their region within two to five years. Yet only 52 per cent said they were satisfied with the options currently available in the market. That mismatch between demand and supply helps explain why ingredient suppliers are racing to fill the gap. Brands want materials that can support sustainability narratives, but they are not willing to sacrifice product performance or user experience. The result is a tighter brief for raw material makers, especially in categories such as skincare and sun care, where consumer scrutiny is high and product claims are closely watched. Lauren Leonard , global market development manager at Eastman, said consumers increasingly expect skin care and sun care products to deliver sustainability benefits alongside strong performance. She added that formulators need ingredients that can balance those priorities while navigating changing regulations, and described SK1N10 as a multifunctional biodegradable option. Regulatory positioning adds to the pitch Beyond performance, Eastman is also leaning on regulatory positioning. The company says SK1N10 is not treated as a synthetic polymer microparticle under EU Regulation 2023/2055 because it meets biodegradability criteria and is sourced under Eastman’s wood pulp sourcing policy. That distinction matters because microplastic restrictions have pushed manufacturers to reassess the materials used in powders, exfoliants and other particulate ingredients. A non-nano, readily biodegradable alternative gives brands another route to reformulate without being forced into a compromise on texture or finish. Eastman also says the ingredient offers an alternative to conventional microparticles such as polymethyl methacrylate and nylon-12 , while giving formulators another option alongside silica and traditional cellulose powders. The timing is significant for a personal care sector that is under pressure from both consumers and regulators. Sustainability claims are now part of the commercial conversation, but they only hold value if the ingredient can perform in real formulations and scale across product lines. That is the space Eastman is trying to occupy with its latest launch. What the launch signals for the market For the broader ingredients market, SK1N10 underscores how the next wave of innovation is likely to be judged. Suppliers are no longer competing only on technical performance or cost. They are also competing on sensory benefits, biodegradability, sourcing credentials and how easily an ingredient can fit into existing manufacturing systems. If Eastman’s claims hold up in commercial formulations, the micropowder could appeal to brands looking to refresh skincare and sunscreen ranges without rewriting their entire product architecture. The bigger takeaway is that biodegradable ingredients are moving from a niche sustainability play to a practical formulation tool, especially in categories where consumer feel and regulatory pressure meet. As brands look for ways to improve product experience while reducing environmental baggage, ingredients like SK1N10 may become part of a new baseline rather than a premium add-on. For now, Eastman is betting that the market is ready for a powder that can do both jobs at once.
